report:
### Conclusion

Your skepticism is well-supported. While conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) showed dramatic fat-loss results in early animal studies, human clinical evidence demonstrates that CLA supplements are largely ineffective for targeted abdominal fat loss and body weight management.

### Key Evidence

1. **Minimal Effect Size:** Meta-analyses of human randomized clinical trials reveal that CLA yields only a trivial reduction in body fat mass—averaging under 0.1 kg per week—which plateaus over time and lacks clinical relevance (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-011-0253-9).
2. **Ineffective for Abdominal Adiposity:** Systematic reviews evaluating anthropometric outcomes confirm that CLA supplementation does not produce meaningful reductions in waist circumference or spot-reduce abdominal fat compared to placebos (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366).
3. **Biological Differences:** Research indicates CLA interacts far more weakly with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) in human tissue than in rodents, failing to trigger appreciable fat oxidation (https://examine.com/supplements/conjugated-linoleic-acid/research/).

In summary, the claim that CLA supplements reduce abdominal fat is false based on current scientific consensus.
